content: The term Feldsher (Russian/Cyrillic: Фельдшер) referred to a category of medical or healthcare professionals in the Soviet Union who were primarily responsible for delivering a wide range of medical services, particularly in rural areas. These individuals were trained in undergraduate medical or health profession schools and were tasked with providing preventive and primary care services. They were also expected to refer more complex or severe cases to higher-level medical institutions for further management. The word Feldsher originally means barber and has its roots in the barber-surgeons of the Russian Army, a practice that dates back to the 1600s. This model of rural primary care delivery later served as a partial inspiration for China's Barefoot Doctors program. The term Feldsher itself is derived from the German word Feldscher, which was coined in the 15th century. Feldscher translates to field doctor (with Feld meaning field and Scher meaning doctor) and was historically used to describe medieval barber-surgeons. These barber-surgeons functioned as field surgeons for the German and Swiss Landsknecht mercenaries until formal military medical services were established by Prussia in the early 18th century. The concept and terminology were subsequently introduced to Russia by Prussian officers and nobility. In the Soviet Union, the role of the Feldsher (Фельдшер) as a healthcare profession was comparable to that of Physician Assistants or Nurse Practitioners in the United States.
